newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top German guerrilla suspect said ready to give up.
newsitem.headline: Top German guerrilla suspect said ready to give up.

text.p: The top suspect in one of Germany's most spectacular political killings says in Monday's edition of the weekly Der Spiegel that he is ready to surrender, helping to close one of the most traumatic chapters in German post-war history.

Christoph Seidler, wanted for the 1989 car-bomb assassination of Deutsche Bank chief executive Alfred Herrhausen by the left-wing Red Army Faction (RAF) guerrilla group, told the magazine he hoped to clear his name by turning himself in.
Seidler acknowledged he had been in touch with the RAF, once known as the Baader-Meinhof Gang, in the 1980s but added: "I never had anything to do with any RAF operation in concrete terms."

Seidler, whose face appears on wanted posters in every post office and police station in Germany, says he spent the years between 1987 and 1992 in Lebanon. Last year he made contact with the anti-extremist Office for the Protection of the Constitution to present evidence in his defence.

He said he hoped the end of the emotionally and politically charged atmosphere of the 1970s and 1980s, when the RAF was battling the German establishment with spectacular killings and abductions, would now allow him a fair hearing.
News of Seidler's move came on the eve of an expected verdict on Tuesday in what will almost certainly be one of the last major trials of a leading RAF figure -- Birgit Hogefeld.

She is accused of murder and attempted murder in connection with an attack on a U.S. airbase in Frankfurt in 1985 and the failed assassination in 1988 of Hans Tietmeyer, then a finance ministry official and now president of the German central bank.

The attacks of the 1970s and 1980s, carried out at a time of left-wing intellectual ferment and the East-West tension of the superpower arms race, claimed over 50 lives and forced Germany to turn its institutions into virtual fortresses.
Hogefeld told the court that the increasingly entrenched attitudes of both sides had contributed to a spiral of violence, and that the RAF now belonged to "a bygone era" and should dissolve itself.

Hogefeld, arrested in June 1993 in a shoot-out in a railway station in Bad Kleinen, said she now considered the Frankfurt attack "horrific and deeply inhuman" and that the armed struggle had been an error.
The end of the Cold War not only deprived the RAF of much of its ideological impetus. It also flushed out 10 RAF members who were given refuge in East Germany by the communist regime.
Many of the earlier generation of RAF leaders have now been released or pardoned.
All the nine who remain in jail now reject the use of violence for political ends, even if it is hardly out of affection for the system they had declared war on.
"We were very much like those we were fighting, and became more and more like them over time," Hogefeld told the court.
